# Could he pet the yak if he turned around on the spot?

**Short answer: No. He would be facing the yak, but it would still be roughly 1.5–2
metres beyond his fingertips, with the pen fence in between. He would have to take a
step or two along the rail (or the yak would have to swing its head toward him) before
he could touch it.**

## Who and where

The man in question is at the upper right of the frame: red/orange T‑shirt, blue denim
knee‑length shorts, back to the camera (his back pockets are visible, no face). He is
standing *outside* the animal pen — the red pipe rail of the pen passes in front of his
shorts and occludes them, so he is on the far side of that rail, in the line of visitors
who are queued along the pen's right‑hand fence. Behind him is a white picket fence and
the rest of the fairground.

The yak is inside the pen, standing on the bedded dirt, facing right, with its head
lowered and turned roughly toward that same right‑hand fence. Its muzzle, halter and
horns are close to the fence line, and the wire‑mesh panel of that fence is visible
directly behind its jaw and nose.

## Why the answer is "no" despite how it looks

In the flat 2‑D picture his legs and the yak's head almost touch, so the intuitive
reaction is "yes". That is a depth illusion. The scale cues say otherwise:

- The yak's head is enormous in the frame (about 200 px from poll to muzzle for a head
  that is roughly 45–50 cm long), while the man's entire hip width spans only about 95 px
  for roughly 40 cm. That makes the image scale at the yak's head close to twice the
  scale at the man, which means the yak's head is only a bit more than half as far from
  the camera as he is.
- Reconstructing the scene from the ground plane (calibrated against the yak's height at
  the withers, its hoof positions, and people standing on visible ground in the
  background) puts the yak's head about 2.2–2.6 m from the camera and the man about
  4.0–4.2 m from the camera, both of them essentially on the same line as the right‑hand
  fence.
- The resulting gap between him and the nearest part of the yak — the tip of the far
  horn and the top of its head — comes out at roughly 1.7–2.0 m; to the poll/forehead it
  is about 1.9–2.0 m. Even on the most generous set of assumptions the gap does not drop
  below about 1.0–1.2 m.

An adult's reach is about 0.7–0.8 m from a standing position, and perhaps 1.1–1.2 m if
he leans hard over a waist‑high rail. So he would be short by something like half a
metre, and quite possibly closer to a full metre.

## Two things that make it look closer than it is

- Another visitor's bare arm (with a wristwatch) hangs down in the picture right next to
  the yak's poll and looks like it is petting the animal. Measuring that hand (hand
  length, watch face) puts it at the visitors' distance from the camera, about 4 m —
  i.e. roughly 1.5–1.8 m *behind* the yak's head, not on it. It only overlaps the yak in
  projection.
- Feet of other visitors are visible through the wire mesh just behind and below the
  yak's jaw, again purely an overlap in the image. Those people are nearer to the yak's
  head than the red‑shirted man is — they are further forward in the queue along the
  fence — and even they would need a long stretch of about a metre to reach it.

## Other things in the way

- He is behind the pen railing, so he cannot simply walk straight at the yak; he would
  have to reach over/through the rail, which costs him reach rather than gaining it.
- There is also a wire‑mesh panel on that stretch of fence, sitting between the yak's
  head and the visitors' side, which further limits how far a hand can be pushed through.
- His orientation is fine, though: he is currently facing away from the pen, and turning
  180° would leave the yak's head and horns ahead of him and slightly to his right, and
  noticeably lower than his shoulders (the yak's poll is only about 0.9–1.0 m off the
  ground because its head is down, versus shoulders at about 1.4 m). So he would be
  looking straight at it — just not able to touch it.

## Bottom line

Turning around in place would put the yak in clear view and in the right direction, but
not within reach. The yak's head sits roughly a metre and a half to two metres away from
his position along the fence line, on the other side of the pen rail and mesh, so from
that exact spot he could not pet it. A step or two forward along the railing — or the
yak lifting and swinging its head toward him — would be needed to close the gap.
